claim: Two gaps are open in the healthcare audit of a five-person household. No eye-care provider is captured at all, so none has been graded. And there is no recorded plan for care outside routine hours — no urgent-care preference, no chosen emergency room, nothing for after-hours or weekend need. The three practitioners the book does name are a doctor, the children's dentist and the garage. Both gaps are the kind of dependency that is discovered under pressure rather than chosen.

evidence:
Read across `alan/book/pages/all-about-alan/topic/pages/` and `.../question/pages/`, searching for an optometrist, eye care, urgent care, an emergency room, after-hours cover, a clinic and a hospital. Nothing matched.

The one page naming practitioners is `trusting-a-person-not-an-institution`: "The local ones I rely on are individual people: my doctor, the children's dentist, the garage." Three, and no fourth.

Two questions circle the gap without filling it. `who-stands-behind-my-practitioners` asks "No second provider stands behind my doctor, the children's dentist or the garage. Who would stand behind each of the three?" and `what-losing-a-practitioner-costs` asks what one leaving would cost. Neither reaches eye care or unscheduled care.

Healthcare otherwise appears only as a category: life-critical in `how-critical-a-dependency-is`, and health cover in `what-leaving-a-dependency-costs-me`.

Not measured: absent from the audit is not the same as absent in life. The household may well use an optometrist nobody has written down, and what is wanted is for the provider to be surfaced rather than chosen. The last sentence of the claim is my own reading.
